title: Where Trump goes now on the big 3: tariffs, Iran war, immigration

blocks.text: World·Analysis

After his party's calamitous loss in the midterms, a looming question is whether U.S. President Donald Trump will shift course on any of his three biggest initiatives since returning to the White House: tariffs, the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.
In surprise White House briefing, Trump downplays key issues that swung voters against Republicans
Trump has come across as somewhat subdued in his public appearances over the past week.

Yet in both his words and actions, Trump has shown defiance in the face of the results, which saw the biggest drop in Republican House candidates' share of the vote in any election since the Watergate scandal of the early 1970s.

He named Stephen Miller — the chief architect of Trump's hard-line immigration policy and the driving force behind much of his unprecedented use of executive orders — as his new chief of staff, the most powerful adviser to the president.
Many observers see the move to elevate Miller as a signal that Trump intends to double down on immigration enforcement rather than ease off.

Then, during an unscheduled briefing Monday afternoon in the White House, Trump mostly brushed aside the issues that drove the vote swing against the Republicans, declaring the war in Iran "effectively over" and describing the U.S. as "doing better than it's ever done before."
With the firm caveat that Trump is often highly unpredictable, here's what analysts expect from the president on his three key initiatives in the wake of the midterms.
Trump loyalists gear up for a fight after Democratic ‘blue-nami’
Tariffs

Trump's long-standing love affair with tariffs is no secret. Even though tariff-driven price increases played a significant role in the Republicans' midterm drubbing, the president appears highly unlikely to toss out the policy entirely.

But some observers do see room for Trump to back down on select tariffs, particularly ones that are politically unpopular, as tariffs on Canadian goods proved to be in border states like Michigan and Maine during the election campaign.

blocks.text: Barbara Weisel, an international trade and investment policy adviser, says there's potential for Trump's team to fine-tune its tariffs, using them in a more strategic and targeted way.

"The scale of the Democratic wave and public anger may prompt the administration to rethink its approach, and it can do so without completely abandoning Trump’s beloved tariffs," Weisel wrote in a post-midterm article published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Drew Fagan, professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, says much will depend on whether Trump and his top advisers "actually want to solve the problems that they've created."

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, seen here with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Sept. 28, has been one of the chief backers of Trump's tariff strategy. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"He's in denial with regard to the degree to which voters saw the economy, inflation, the weakness of their paycheques versus cost as the fundamental issue, and tariffs were part of this," Fagan told CBC News Network on Monday.

One data point that could signal whether Trump intends to shift his trade agenda will be whether any of the top advocates for tariffs in his administration either leave or get pushed out, chiefly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick or U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
War with Iran
Senior members of the Trump administration, including to some extent the president himself, are acknowledging the war's impact on gas prices hurt Republicans in the midterms.
While Trump and his team continue to defend the decision to go to war with Iran, they are signaling they want it to end. However their path to doing so remains anything but clear.

blocks.text: "We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," Trump said during the Monday briefing.
Trump has said for months that the war would end soon.
The question becomes whether the end will be found through a peace deal or military escalation.
Trump names hardliner Stephen Miller chief of staff after midterm blowout

A diplomatic agreement could "reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged U.S. national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects and his personal legacy," said William F. Wechsler, a former Pentagon official responsible for special operations and combating terrorism.

"The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come," Wechsler wrote in a piece for the Atlantic Council, a Washington, D.C.-based think-tank.
Immigration enforcement
In his interview with 60 Minutes, recorded Friday, Trump said the administration may have been too tough in its deportation policy.
But when asked during Monday's briefing whether he has told Miller he wants changes to immigration enforcement, Trump's response suggests there won't be a substantial shift.
"We have a very strong deportation policy," Trump said. "My policy hasn't changed."

blocks.text: Earlier this year, after federal agents in Minneapolis shot and killed two American citizens, the administration toned down the high-profile, aggressive nature of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics.

However, ICE actually stepped up its overall pace of detentions to hit record highs in the summer, according to analysis by the Deportation Data Project, based at the University of California Berkeley and UCLA.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents detain a man outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs building during a protest in Portland, Ore., in June 2025. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)
Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University, is skeptical that Trump will move in any significant way toward softening his immigration policy.

"It doesn't seem likely, not with this decision to have Stephen Miller running the show," Binder said Monday in a post-midterm briefing organized by the Brookings Institution, a think-tank in Washington.

blocks.text: Yemisi Egbewole, who served as chief of staff in former president Joe Biden's press office, says it's hard to reconcile Trump's appointment of Miller as chief of staff with his claim to 60 Minutes that he's willing to reach a compromise with the Democrats on immigration.
"That really speaks to the duality of the president. He says one thing, but then his actions deliver another totally different result," Egbewole told CBC News Network on Monday.
"There are ways to find common ground, but the president has to drive the conversation there and not let Stephen Miller enact his own agenda," she said.

Trump's willingness to make deals with the Democrats on immigration — or any other major policies — is almost certain to dwindle if the party follows through on threats to launch Congressional investigations into allegations of corruption against the president's family and inner circle.
